newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, Chernomyrdin to mull new cabinet line-up.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, Chernomyrdin to mull new cabinet line-up.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin were due to meet on Thursday to discuss a radical shake-up of the government intended to jump-start stalled market reforms.

The meeting, which the presidential press service said would start at 1 p.m. (1000 GMT), might herald an announcement later on Thursday of a new cabinet line-up, ending a week of high suspense and uncertainty in Russian politics.

Yeltsin ordered Chernomyrdin to reorganise his government after giving an annual state-of-the-nation speech on Thursday in which he blasted its failure to tackle Russia's economic and social problems, including chronic delays in the payment of wages and pensions.

Apart from Chernomyrdin, a trusted Yeltsin ally who epitomises Russian reforms to the outside world, the only man guaranteed to keep his job is the newly appointed First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais.

Chubais will be the sole first deputy premier in the new line-up -- there are four now -- and the number of ministers will also be cut, helping to reduce a bloated government bureaucracy little changed from Soviet times.

Interfax news agency, quoting "well-informed sources", said the heads of most "power ministries" -- defence and interior ministries and security organs that answer directly to Yeltsin -- were unlikely to be changed, probably with the exception of Defence Minister Igor Rodionov.
Chernomyrdin said on Wednesday his new cabinet, which he has promised to present by the end of the week, would be younger and more professional and include market-minded reformers.
He added that most new ministers would be under 50 and have administrative experience.

Yegor Gaidar, who as Chernomyrdin's predecessor launched Russia's first market reforms in 1992, said on Thursday he did not expect to be a member of the new government but said it would have no alternative to radical reforms, whoever joined it.
"I am ready to help (a new cabinet) insofar as I am able... I would cooperate intellectually," Interfax quoted Gaidar as telling a gathering of students.

He blamed the lack of consistent market reforms for budget problems which leave millions of workers and pensioners unpaid for months on end and said Chubais' appointment was a "correct step on dragging Russia out of crisis".

Architect of Russia's tough privatisation drive in 1992-1996, Chubais is a hate figure for the communist and ultra-nationalist opposition who accuse him of selling off Russian state firms too cheaply.
They also cannot forgive the youthful liberal for helping to spearhead Yeltsin's re-election campaign last summer. Until now Chubais has been in charge of the Kremlin administration.

In a non-binding resolution approved on Wednesday, the communist-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament condemned Chubais' nomination as "a provocation to public opinion" and said the reshuffle would lead Russia to ruin.

But the deputies made clear they wanted to take part in the reshuffle, urging Yeltsin to hold consultations with parliament, and many of them were quick to stress that there was no word about any attempt to topple Chernomyrdin.
"We are not stoking passion, it is just another document similar to those which the Duma had passed before," a leader of the Communist faction Anatoly Lukyanov told NTV commercial television.
The new government will face its first challenge on March 27, when trade unions plan to hold a nationwide day of strikes.
Union leaders said on Wednesday the government reshuffle would not change their plans.
